# Phandanajātaka (Ja 475)

**ID:** Ja 475
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Phandanajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Lion and the Boxwood Tree
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja475
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul12.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Phandanajātaka* (Ja 475) is a narrative within the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The story is set on the bank of the river Rohiṇī, delivered by the Buddha to his quarreling kinsmen to illustrate the catastrophic results of mutual hostility, a background detailed more extensively in the *Kuṇālajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Fausböll 1891]. In the tale, a carpenter seeks timber in the forest to fashion cart wheels; a black lion holding a grudge against a tree deity recommends felling the *phandana* tree, whereupon the tree urges the woodcutter to slay the lion for its hide to wrap the wheel rim, leading to reciprocal destruction [Fausböll 1887; Fausböll 1891; Sujato 2011]. The Bodhisatta, appearing as an observing forest deity, warns against finding faults and inciting mutual ruin, exhorting unity (*sāmaggi*) [Fausböll 1887; Schmithausen 2009].

The text has featured prominently in scholarly and traditional discussions on plant sentience in early Buddhism [Schmithausen 1991; Schmithausen 2009]. In the verses of the Jātaka (Jā IV 207–210), the tree itself speaks to the woodcutter; this passage is explicitly cited and debated in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.5, *Rukkhaacetanābhāvapañha*), which seeks to reconcile the narrative with the insentience (*acetana*) of plants by explaining that it was the resident tree deity, not the tree itself, who spoke [SuttaCentral; Schmithausen 1991; Schmithausen 2009].

SuttaCentral identifies thematic and verse parallels across several Buddhist traditions, notably verses shared with the Taṇhāvagga of the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 337), the *Theragāthā* (Thag 6.5), the *Mahākapijātaka* (Ja 516), Chinese versions of the *Dharmapada* (T 210, T 212, T 213), the *Gāndhārī Dharmapada*, the Patna Dharmapada, and the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches the text extensively with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and reports computational alignments with Tibetan texts (including the *Vinaya-uttaragrantha*, *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā*, and *Jātakamālā*) as well as the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
